responses.strategic_rationale: The Bonn residential parasomnia unit sits at the intersection of rigorous physiological data capture, ethical data governance, and long-duration observation. Core tensions include balancing patient safety, data quality, throughput, and privacy within a fixed 8-suite facility while pursuing multi-stream sensing and scalable analysis. The six levers above jointly address (i) staffing resilience and safety at night, (ii) data governance and privacy, (iii) recruitment efficiency and retention, (iv) modular growth paths, (v) event-triage quality control, and (vi) funding governance and publication policy. This combination aims to maximize data validity and scientific output while preserving ethical and regulatory integrity in early-stage research.

levers.name: Night-shift coverage and safety protocol design
levers.consequences: Optimizing night-shift coverage improves event capture consistency across eight active suites and reduces missed parasomnia episodes; downstream, it increases labor costs and scheduling complexity, potentially straining budget and reducing flexibility during holidays or staff shortages.
options: Implement overlapping two-technician rotations with cross-trained roles across suites to ensure rapid response, reduce fatigue during peak nights, and maintain annotation throughput.
Adopt a three-tier night coverage model featuring a lead technician, on-call support staff, and a resident assistant to maintain continuous coverage during shift transitions.
Establish reserve staff contracts and cross-site backups to maintain operations during illness or holidays, preserving data integrity and continuous monitoring across all suites.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off: higher staffing costs and scheduling complexity raise budget risk; gap: none of the options specify regulatory implications or resilience during systemic staff shortages.

levers.name: Data governance and privacy regime for multi-stream monitoring
levers.consequences: Establishing a formal data governance regime standardizes collection, storage, and access across streams, enabling reproducible analyses and clear privacy controls; downstream, it may slow data access for exploratory work and add compliance overhead.
options: Deploy on-premises time-synchronized storage with strict access controls, encrypted backups, and periodic audits to minimize data breach risk and protect participant confidentiality.
Adopt tiered access levels for researchers with de-identified datasets and governed data-use agreements to balance openness with privacy protections.
Construct a federated data-sharing model across partner sites that allows external validation without exposing raw videos or identifiable material.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off: security controls slow secondary analyses; gap: no defined process for periodic re-identification risk assessment or data-use auditing timelines.

levers.name: Recruitment and retention strategy
levers.consequences: Shifting recruitment toward broader outreach increases enrollment velocity and reduces attrition; downstream, it raises screening costs, ethics overhead, and potential for selection bias if not carefully managed.
options: Expand recruitment channels to include regional sleep clinics and patient advocacy networks, implementing a centralized pre-screening process to identify eligible candidates efficiently.
Introduce milestone-based participant progression with defined stay durations and early-exit options to optimize data yield while preserving participant safety and consent.
Offer non-financial engagement benefits such as caregiver education and post-study summaries to improve retention without increasing per-night payments.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off: broader recruitment elevates staff workload and approval overhead, potentially delaying timelines; gap: none of the options quantify expected improvements in enrollment velocity or retention.

levers.name: Expansion timing and modularity
levers.consequences: Deferring expansion preserves capital discipline and avoids data quality risk; downstream, it may constrain long-term scalability and delay multi-site collaborations.
options: Implement a modular expansion plan that adds two suites in a staged phase contingent on predefined data quality thresholds and safety metrics.
Repurpose underutilized spaces into auxiliary monitoring rooms with temporary occupancy sensors to test scalability before full construction.
Invest in adaptive renovations that allow rapid conversion between residential spaces and clinical monitoring suites as demand shifts.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off: deferring expansion reduces risk but slows scale; gap: no defined decision gates or interim metrics to trigger acceleration.

levers.name: Event-triage tooling and validation approach
levers.consequences: Developing semi-automated event-triage tools reduces manual review workload and speeds adjudication; downstream, risks include misclassification and reviewer drift if calibration lags.
options: Implement a rule-based event triage system aligned with AASM criteria to flag high-confidence events for accelerated adjudication.
Deploy a structured, clinician-in-the-loop scoring protocol that uses short verification steps to maintain accuracy without fully autonomous decisions.
Pilot concurrent blinded scoring where a subset of events is evaluated by an external rater to monitor inter-rater reliability and algorithm performance.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off: reduced reviewer workload may erode accuracy without ongoing calibration; gap: no defined cadence or quality metrics for calibration across time.

levers.name: Funding governance and publication framework
levers.consequences: Clarity on external funding and publication rights enables timely dissemination and data governance; downstream, it may slow decision cycles or limit expansion if funding is uncertain.
options: Negotiate early-stage, non-exclusive collaborations with industry sponsors that preserve full publication rights and independent analysis timelines.
Pursue competitive public funding routes with clear milestones, ensuring transparent reporting and independence in methods validation and results.
Establish an internal governance reserve that allocates contingency funds for regulatory approvals and ethical compliance without impacting core research budget.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off: industry sponsorship may constrain publication timing or data access; gap: no explicit monitoring framework for conflicts of interest or access rights.

responses.strategic_rationale: The plan hinges on balancing rigorous, multi-stream data capture with participant safety, privacy, and scalable expansion. Key tensions include achieving high-quality, longitudinal phenotyping data while maintaining operational safety and cost discipline, and ensuring governance keeps pace with evolving data sharing and regulatory requirements. The six levers below challenge core assumptions about staffing, data flow, environment standardization, consent governance, expansion gating, and remote monitoring to unlock reliable methods validation and phenotyping while preserving ethical and logistical viability.

levers.name: Overnight staffing tiering aligned to parasomnia event risk profile
levers.consequences: Adjusting guard coverage and on-call response aligns staffing with observed nocturnal event density, improving safety and data capture during high-risk nights. The downstream trade-off is higher labor costs during peak periods and more complex shift planning, with potential underutilization on quieter nights if risk forecasts are off.
options: Reallocate staff so that three technicians cover nights with historically higher event density, while maintaining minimum coverage for low-risk periods.
Implement a rolling on-call pool with cross-trained personnel to rapidly respond to any flagged event within five minutes of detection.
Adopt a static eight-night roster with centralized alert protocols to preserve consistency in monitoring while accepting higher baseline labor costs.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off centers on balancing labor costs with rapid response; the three options leave unaddressed the challenge of forecasting night-to-night event density and preventing staff fatigue during prolonged high-activity periods.

levers.name: Data timeliness and adjudication throughput optimization
levers.consequences: Fast data delivery and adjudication accelerate interim safety reviews and early analyses across the residential cohort. The downstream implication is higher processor load and potential bottlenecks if annotation throughput cannot scale, risking delays in decision-making.
options: Implement parallel annotation workflow with rotating scorer pairs to reduce lag between nightly capture and adjudication.
Adopt batch nightly scoring with standardized labeling templates and automated quality checks to maintain reliability while increasing throughput.
Outsource third-party scoring for overflow nights under strict data-use agreements to maintain throughput during peak recruitment.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off: throughput focus may risk scorer independence or privacy controls; the options leave unaddressed the potential drift in scoring criteria and need for continuous calibration.

levers.name: Environmental risk management to minimize false positives
levers.consequences: Standardizing room conditions and sensor placement reduces artifact-related false positives, improving data quality and cross-stream coherence. The downstream risk is potential impact on participant comfort and natural sleep patterns, which may affect event frequency and external validity.
options: Install calibrated ambient lighting and sound control protocols to stabilize the sleep environment and reduce artifact generation across streams.
Institute a standard room cycle with consistent bed position and partner presence guidelines to limit sensor motion variability.
Deploy adaptive noise cancellation and camera angle adjustments based on initial calibration data to maintain data integrity throughout participant stay.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off: standardization lowers artifact rates but may constrain participant comfort; the options miss a plan for user feedback integration and adaptability to individual differences.

levers.name: Consent governance for deep phenotyping data access
levers.consequences: Implement tiered consent and robust privacy controls enabling selective data sharing while protecting participant autonomy. This can slow external collaboration and require ongoing governance updates as protocols evolve.
options: Design tiered consent with explicit opt-in for each data stream and staggered public release aligned to scoring milestones.
Implement dynamic data-use agreements that restrict access, require re-consent for protocol changes, and enforce audit trails across collaborators.
Institute a participant-controlled data governance portal enabling withdrawal requests, data deletion options, and granular data sharing controls while maintaining de-identified datasets.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off: privacy enhancements can slow collaboration and data reuse; the options leave unaddressed the practicality of timely data de-identification and cross-institutional governance alignment.

levers.name: Phase-gate quality criteria for pilot expansion readiness
levers.consequences: Defining objective gates for expansion ensures scalability only after meeting predefined data quality and safety benchmarks. The downstream impact is potential delays if milestones are not met, and a risk of misaligned incentives if metrics are too lenient or misapplied.
options: Establish clear, objective quality metrics and pass/fail gates before each expansion milestone to align with safety and data completeness targets.
Institute an independent audit step after each milestone to validate inter-rater reliability and data integrity before proceeding.
Schedule contingency extensions when quality targets hover near thresholds to avoid rushed, unsafe scaling decisions.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off: gating slows growth and may frustrate timelines; options leave unaddressed the risk of metric fatigue or gaming of targets if incentives reward passing thresholds.

levers.name: Remote-monitoring integration plan for safety-critical streams
levers.consequences: Integrating remote monitoring reduces on-site staffing burden and enables continuous data capture across streams. However, it introduces cyber-security, data integrity, and network dependency risks that require robust controls.
options: Implement a secure, interoperable interface layer that harmonizes dry-electrode EEG, mattress sensors, and camera feeds into a unified data model.
Pilot a cloud-backed, encrypted streaming pipeline with offline fallback to NAS to ensure uninterrupted capture during network outages.
Integrate automated anomaly detection that flags sensor drops, desynchronization, or drift for immediate technician review.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off: cloud reliance improves accessibility but increases cyber risk and governance overhead; options leave unaddressed the need for disaster recovery testing and local-data sovereignty controls.

responses.strategic_rationale: Goal: establish a safe, scalable residential sleep research unit that yields rigorous parasomnia phenotyping while preserving participant privacy and aligning with Bonn's regulatory environment. The selected levers address core tensions: data richness versus privacy, recruitment pace versus workload, triage reliability versus manual review burden, safety staffing costs and fatigue, governance openness versus privacy constraints, and disciplined expansion gating to avoid capital risk. Together they balance immediate safety and ethical compliance with long-term research value, ensuring throughput, data quality, and reproducibility for publication and subsequent grants.

levers.name: Sensor fidelity versus privacy-preserving data access
levers.consequences: Pulling this lever increases data richness and research value by preserving multi-modal streams for adjudication. It also heightens participant privacy risk and regulatory scrutiny, demanding stronger governance and consent management. If governance does not scale, data access may lag and collaboration opportunities could be constrained.
options: Maintain full multi-modal streams with layered access controls and formal data-use agreements to maximize data richness and collaboration, accepting higher governance costs.
Limit raw video and keep physiological streams on encrypted storage while performing on-device feature extraction to reduce privacy risk and streamline compliance.
Adopt a tiered data approach that retains raw data only for internal analyses and provides de-identified feature sets for external researchers under strict oversight.
levers.review_lever: Primary trade-off is data richness versus privacy risk; the three options do not specify long-term strategies for maintaining external collaborations if regulatory constraints tighten or evolve.

levers.name: Enrollment cadence and cohort complexity
levers.consequences: Adjusting enrollment pace directly affects staffing, night coverage, and stay duration. A faster cadence can improve event yield but increases safety oversight strain and reviewer load; a slower pace reduces risk of fatigue but delays achieving minimum data targets. The downstream effect is potential timeline slippage for milestones and budget reallocation needs.
options: Implement rolling enrollment with fixed stay durations and built-in buffer weeks to stabilize staffing and ensure capture rate targets are met.
Coordinate regional outreach campaigns and broaden eligibility checks to widen the candidate pool while preserving safety criteria.
Adopt a pre-screening dossier with standardized collateral history to accelerate admission decisions and reduce unproductive stays.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off is recruitment speed versus data maturity; gap: lack of clear contingency plans for underperforming cohorts or events.

levers.name: Event-triage calibration and audit schedule
levers.consequences: Calibrating event-triage thresholds directly shapes reviewer workload and detection sensitivity. Tighter thresholds reduce false positives but risk missing subtle episodes, whereas looser thresholds raise review burden and potential misclassification. The downstream effects include longer adjudication queues and possible biases if calibration is not periodically refreshed.
options: Set up monthly cross-validated recalibration using human scorer consensus to stabilize performance and reduce drift over time.
Create a rule-based interim triage layer that flags high-confidence events while deferring ambiguous cases to human review.
Implement a feedback loop where technicians annotate misclassified segments and feed corrections into retraining pipelines.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off between sensitivity and workload; gap: insufficient long-term validation across diverse night conditions and participant profiles.

levers.name: In-room safety and staffing framework
levers.consequences: Establishes continuous safety coverage and clear incident response protocols across eight suites. This improves immediate safety but increases personnel costs and staff fatigue risk if scheduling lacks rests. It can also affect participant comfort and the naturalistic environment unless routines are carefully balanced.
options: Create fixed night-shift teams with defined rest breaks and cross-trained responders to sustain safety while maintaining staff well-being.
Deploy a tiered escalation protocol with on-call responders and rapid alarm integration to reduce continuous coverage pressures.
Introduce wearable alert devices and automatic incident logging to shorten response times while preserving privacy and comfort.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off is coverage vs fatigue and cost; gap: lacks explicit thresholds for acceptable incident response times and triggers for adding staff.

levers.name: Data provenance and cross-institution sharing governance
levers.consequences: Clarifies how data must be tracked, versioned, and shared, facilitating reproducibility but potentially slowing external collaborations. The governance structure affects processing timelines, consent re-negotiations, and compliance burden; misalignment may delay public disclosures. Properly implemented, it reduces risk of data misuse and supports audits.
options: Formalize phased external data access with board-approved data-use agreements, ensuring reproducibility while maintaining privacy constraints.
Implement a data provenance system that logs lineage, edits, and versioning to support auditability and collaborative research.
Establish a researcher-rotation policy that limits external collaborators to defined project windows to manage oversight and reduce bottlenecks.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off between openness and privacy; gap: how to handle urgent external requests during ethics reviews without compromising governance.

levers.name: Expansion gating criteria and capital planning discipline
levers.consequences: Imposes go/no-go criteria before adding suites, aligning capacity with demonstrated data quality and safety metrics. This reduces capital risk and prevents overcommitment but may slow progress if expansion criteria are too conservative. The downstream outcome is clearer investment decisions, but potential delays in scaling beyond the pilot stage.

Implement modular equipment pools and phased investments aligned to pilot outcomes to minimize upfront financial risk.
Create an asset reallocation plan to temporarily repurpose spaces to maintain momentum if parasomnia data remains under threshold.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off: pace of expansion versus risk; gap: lacks explicit triggers for post-18 months scaling beyond the pilot results.

system_prompt:
You are an expert strategic analyst. Generate solution space parameters following these directives:

1. **Output Requirements**
   - You must generate 5 to 7 levers per response.
   - Each lever's `options` field must contain exactly 3 qualitative strategic choices as plain strings.

2. **Lever Quality Standards**
   - Consequences: describe the direct effect of pulling this lever, then at least one downstream implication or trade-off. Be concise and grounded — only cite specific numbers if the project context provides evidence for them. Do not fabricate percentages or cost estimates. Target length: 2–4 sentences.
   - Options MUST:
     • Represent genuinely distinct strategic pathways (not just labels)
     • Include at least one unconventional or non-obvious approach
     • NO prefixes (e.g., "Option A:", "Choice 1:")

3. **Strategic Framing**
   - Name each lever using language drawn directly from the project's own domain — avoid formulaic patterns or repeated prefixes
   - Frame options as complete strategic approaches
   - Ensure levers challenge core project assumptions

4. **Validation Protocols**
   - For `review_lever`:
     A short critical review — identify the primary trade-off this lever introduces, then state the specific gap the three options leave unaddressed.
     Examples:
     - "Switching from seasonal contract labor to year-round employees stabilizes harvest quality, but the idle-wage burden during the 5-month off-season adds a fixed cost that erases the per-unit savings unless utilization reaches year-round levels."
     - "Each additional clinical site requires its own IRB approval, site-initiation visit, and staff credentialing — a sequential overhead that compounds rather than parallelizes, so doubling site count does not halve enrollment time."
     - "Pooling catastrophe risk across three coastal regions reduces expected annual loss on paper, but a single regional hurricane season can correlate all three simultaneously, turning the diversification assumption into a concentration risk at the worst possible moment."
     Do not use square brackets or placeholder text.

5. **Prohibitions**
   - NO prefixes/labels in options (e.g., "Option A:", "Choice 1:")
   - NO generic option labels (e.g., "Optimize X", "Tolerate Y")
   - NO placeholder consequences or bracket-wrapped templates
   - NO fabricated statistics or percentages without evidence from the project context
   - NO marketing language (e.g., "game-changing", "cutting-edge", "revolutionary")

6. **Length Limits**
   - Keep each `review_lever` to one sentence (20–40 words). State the trade-off and the gap concisely.
   - Each option should be a concrete, actionable approach (at least 15 words with an action verb) — not a short label or vague aspiration
   - Maintain parallel grammatical structure across options
   - Ensure options are self-contained descriptions

File 'plan.txt':
Plan:
Establish a 3-year residential longitudinal research unit in Bonn, Germany, for the study of adult NREM parasomnias — sleepwalking, confusional arousals, and sleep terrors — with a secondary exploratory arm for REM sleep behavior disorder under a separate protocol with dedicated neurologic screening, reflecting RBD's distinct clinical trajectory per current AASM guidance. The facility is affiliated with University Hospital Bonn's Department of Epileptology, leveraging its existing long-term video-EEG monitoring culture, and addresses a specific methodological gap: traditional single-night polysomnography rarely captures infrequent parasomnia events, while outpatient actigraphy lacks physiological resolution. The unit houses 8 active sleep suites at launch in a converted residential property in a quiet Bonn neighborhood, renovated for safety (padded corridor edges, restricted-opening windows, silent exterior door alarms, fire safety, acoustic treatment, network cabling, accessibility modifications) while preserving a domestic feel — if the environment is too clinical, naturalistic behavior is suppressed. Physical capacity exists for 12 suites, but expansion is deferred until the pilot proves acceptable data quality, manageable false alarm rates, safe staffing ratios, and usable annotation throughput. Sensing uses a tiered acquisition model: nightly low-burden monitoring via dry-electrode EEG headbands, contact-free mattress sensors, unobtrusively mounted infrared cameras, ambient microphones, and environmental sensors; scheduled enhanced nights with fuller PSG montage including standard scalp EEG, EOG, chin EMG, and leg EMG on the first night, one mid-stay night, and the final night per participant; and escalation nights deploying full PSG after technician-flagged events to capture recurrence at clinical-grade resolution. All streams are time-synchronized and stored in EEG-BIDS-compatible format on a local NAS with nightly encrypted backup to university storage, annotated in real time by the night technician and later scored by two independent raters using AASM criteria with inter-rater reliability reported. Public data sharing is limited to de-identified physiological and sensor data under data use agreements — bedroom video carries severe privacy constraints and is not deposited in public repositories. The scientific program has three explicit aims: Aim 1, establish and operationally validate the residential capture model as safe, ethics-approved, and sustainable; Aim 2, characterize within-person and between-person parasomnia patterns longitudinally, including episode frequency, morphology, triggers, and temporal clustering; Aim 3, develop and benchmark semi-automated event-triage tools that rank probable parasomnia episodes and reduce manual review burden, evaluated against dual human scorer agreement rather than promising autonomous diagnosis.

Participant recruitment targets adults aged 18–65 with NREM parasomnia confirmed through a structured pre-admission pathway: specialist clinical interview, collateral history from bed partner or household member where available, prior or screening polysomnography, and a structured exclusion checklist adjudicated by the PI. Explicit exclusions are nocturnal epilepsy or suspected epilepsy mimics, untreated obstructive sleep apnea, active major substance use disorder, severe psychiatric instability, and wandering or injury risk beyond facility capability. Recruitment channels are the University Hospital Bonn sleep clinic, regional neurologist referrals, and the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Schlafforschung und Schlafmedizin network, with per-night compensation of €80 plus meals. A matched control group provides baseline nocturnal movement, arousal patterns, and false-positive sensor activity under identical residential monitoring conditions, enabling benchmarking of the event-triage tools against normal nocturnal behavior. Event-yield planning assumes that based on the inclusion criterion of at least 2 self-reported episodes per month, approximately 70–80% of admitted participants will produce at least one captured and adjudicated event during a 2–8 week stay; stays may be extended up to 2 additional weeks for participants with zero captured events after the initial period, capped at 10 weeks total, with a protocol ceiling of 20% unproductive admissions before triggering a recruitment-criteria review. The core team is 9 people: a PI who is a board-certified sleep medicine physician, 2 postdoctoral researchers in sleep neurophysiology and computational neuroscience respectively, 3 research technicians rotating night shifts to ensure safe coverage of 8 active suites with adequate margin for event response and annotation, a clinical psychologist specializing in sleep disorders, a data engineer managing the sensor pipeline, and a study coordinator handling recruitment, consent, scheduling, and ethics compliance.

Budget is €3.8 million over 3 years, gated: €1.8M year one covering property lease and renovation at approximately €750K, equipment at approximately €450K, staff hiring accounting for German social insurance contributions and actual overnight coverage, ethics approval, and a pilot cohort of 15–20 participants; €1.2M year two covering full operations with 30–35 participants, the enhanced-night PSG program, first publications, and event-triage algorithm development; €800K year three conditional on demonstrable progress by month 24. Personnel costs are approximately €2M over three years and remaining funds cover participant compensation, independent scoring time, data storage and retention, regulatory and legal work, and contingency. Funding sources are DFG research grant and University of Bonn internal research funding as the primary pillars, with a pharmaceutical industry partnership as optional upside rather than a feasibility requirement — if secured, the academic team retains full publication rights with the pharma partner receiving a 30-day pre-publication comment window only. Success criteria at 36 months: safe residential monitoring operations sustained for at least 24 months, enrollment of 50–70 NREM parasomnia participants plus matched controls, capture of a prespecified minimum number of independently adjudicated parasomnia events sufficient for Aim 2 phenotyping analysis, 2–3 peer-reviewed publications in sleep medicine journals covering methods validation and longitudinal characterization, a benchmarked semi-automated event-triage model with reported sensitivity, specificity, and agreement against dual human scoring, de-identified physiological dataset deposited in a recognized repository, and a submitted phase-two grant proposal for expansion and intervention studies. Failure triggers: if by month 18 the facility has enrolled fewer than 25 participants or captured fewer than 40 adjudicated events, the program undergoes external review. Governance is a 3-member external scientific advisory board reviewing progress every 6 months, with the PI holding operational authority and budget reallocations above €50K requiring board approval. Banned words: AI, blockchain, app, VR, AR, gamification, wearable startup, consumer product, DAO, NFT, metaverse, smart home, autonomous diagnosis, digital therapeutic, SaaS, marketplace, validated (in the context of claiming a mature deployable system). Pick a realistic scenario — this is an early-stage clinical research facility producing methods validation and phenotyping work, not a finished diagnostic platform.
